name: PowerView - Passwords in AD Descriptions
description: Searches AD user object descriptions for embedded passwords. Admins commonly store temporary or service account passwords in the ADUC 'Description' field for convenience — readable by all authenticated domain users. This is a quick, high-yield credential hunt that requires only read access to AD.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY PASSWORDS END UP IN DESCRIPTIONS ===
The AD 'Description' field on user objects is visible to all domain users (by default).
Admins put passwords there for:
  - New employee account setup ('Temp password: Welcome2021!')
  - Service accounts created by helpdesk ('created by IT - password: Serv1ce!')
  - Legacy accounts ('Old SQL service account - pass: Sql@2018')
  - Test accounts ('Test account - pw: Test1234')

None of these are encrypted or protected — readable by any domain user via LDAP.

=== FILTER FOR HIGH-VALUE HITS ===
Not all descriptions contain passwords. Look for:
  - Keywords: password, pass, pw, pwd, temp, initial, welcome
  - Number patterns: YYYY, seasonal (Spring, Summer, Winter, Fall)
  - Special char patterns that look like passwords

  Get-DomainUser * | select samaccountname,description | Where-Object {$_.description -match 'password|pass|welcome|temp'}

=== LINUX EQUIVALENT ===
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc_ip> -D 'user@domain.local' -w 'pass' \
  -b 'DC=INLANEFREIGHT,DC=LOCAL' '(objectClass=user)' description samaccountname

=== WHAT TO DO WITH FOUND PASSWORDS ===
1. Test directly: evil-winrm -i <dc> -u <account> -p <found_password>
2. Check if account is active and not locked
3. Spray across other accounts (password reuse)
4. Look up account's group membership + AD rights (may be high-priv)

=== COMPUTER OBJECTS TOO ===
Get-DomainComputer * | select name,description | Where-Object {$_.description -ne $null}
Admins sometimes put build info, admin credentials, or config notes on computer objects.

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: The AD user object's Description attribute is readable by all authenticated domain users via LDAP — it's a standard attribute with no restricted ACL by default. Admins routinely store temporary passwords, initial credentials, or notes in the Description field (visible in ADUC) for convenience, without realising it is world-readable by any domain member.
defense.prerequisites: Domain membership (any authenticated user). PowerShell with PowerView, or any LDAP client. No elevated privileges needed.
defense.impact: Plaintext credential discovery for service accounts, admin accounts, or user accounts. Credentials may be current (many admins never clear descriptions after initial setup) and enable immediate authentication, privilege escalation, or lateral movement depending on the account's rights.
defense.detection: No specific Windows Event ID for reading user Description attributes. LDAP audit logging (if enabled via SACL on user objects) would record attribute reads. Large-scale LDAP enumeration of all users with their descriptions in a single query could be flagged by SIEM behavioral analytics. EDR may flag PowerView module loading.
defense.prevention: Audit Description fields across all user objects immediately: Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description | Where-Object {$_.Description -match 'pass|pwd|cred|temp'} | Select Name,Description. Remove any credentials found. Establish a policy prohibiting credential storage in AD attribute fields. Train admins to use approved password vaults (LAPS, CyberArk, Azure Key Vault) for temporary credentials. Schedule recurring automated scans of Description fields.
defense.evasion: A targeted LDAP query against a specific user is completely indistinguishable from normal AD lookup. Even bulk PowerView enumeration generates LDAP traffic that matches legitimate admin activity. No modification is made to any AD object.
defense.misconfiguration: Administrative shortcuts create persistent misconfigurations: passwords stored in AD Description/Info attributes (visible to all users), accounts with PasswordNotRequired flag set (blank passwords allowed), LAPS attribute readable by non-admin groups, gMSA readable by unintended principals, or SYSVOL containing scripts with embedded credentials.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Passwords in AD Description field:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description | Where-Object {$_.Description -ne $null}
# Returns: svc_backup  Description: 'Temp password: Welcome1!'

# PasswordNotRequired flag (UAC 0x20 = PASSWD_NOTREQD):
Get-ADUser -Filter {PasswordNotRequired -eq $true}

# LAPS password readable by Domain Users (misconfigured ACL):
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties ms-Mcs-AdmPwd | Select-Object Name,'ms-Mcs-AdmPwd'
# Should only be readable by admins + specific LAPS readers group
defense.secure_config:
# Remove passwords from Description/Info fields:
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description,Info |
    Where-Object {$_.Description -match 'pass|pwd|temp|welcome'} |
    Set-ADUser -Description $null

# Fix PasswordNotRequired accounts:
Get-ADUser -Filter {PasswordNotRequired -eq $true} |
    Set-ADAccountControl -PasswordNotRequired $false

# LAPS ACL hardening — restrict ms-Mcs-AdmPwd reads:
# Only specific LAPS-Readers security group should have Read on this attribute
# Run: Set-AdmPwdComputerSelfPermission, Set-AdmPwdReadPasswordPermission

# Audit gMSA readers:
Get-ADServiceAccount -Filter * -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword |
    Select-Object Name, PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword
